overviewHtml:
This ungraded knowledge check assesses your understanding of Sartre's and Beauvoir's accounts of consciousness and the body. You'll be asked about pre-reflective consciousness, the look, the three dimensions of the body, the body as situation, and a key difference between Sartre and Beauvoir.

Note: Use this to test yourself, review the feedback on any questions you miss, and retry until you feel confident before moving forward.

forms.stemHtml: While running after a streetcar, what are you conscious of, on Sartre's account?

options.html: Yourself as the one who is running
options.text: Yourself as the one who is running
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. On Sartre's account, there's no "I" in unreflective consciousness. You're conscious of the streetcar, as having-to-be-caught.
Correct! Pre-reflective consciousness is absorbed in its object. The "I" appears only in reflection.

options.html: Nothing, since the running is unconscious
options.text: Nothing, since the running is unconscious
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Pre-reflective consciousness is conscious, and aware of itself non-positionally. Its object is the streetcar.

options.html: Your legs and breathing as bodily objects
options.text: Your legs and breathing as bodily objects
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. While running, you aren't attending to your body as an object. You're conscious of the streetcar, as having-to-be-caught.

forms.stemHtml: A hiker alone in the woods hears a branch snap behind her and suddenly feels herself observed. Does this count as Sartre's "look"?

options.html: No, because she hasn't seen anyone's eyes
options.text: No, because she hasn't seen anyone's eyes
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. For Sartre, the look needn't be literal vision. Footsteps or a rustle can manifest the other as a subject.

options.html: No, because the look requires a judgment of guilt
options.text: No, because the look requires a judgment of guilt
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The look is the other's presence as a subject for whom I'm an object. It doesn't require a judgment of guilt.

options.html: Yes, since a sound can manifest the other as a subject
options.text: Yes, since a sound can manifest the other as a subject
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! For Sartre, the look can be manifested by a rustle of branches or footsteps. What matters is the other's presence as a subject.

options.html: Yes, but only if she later confirms someone was there
options.text: Yes, but only if she later confirms someone was there
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The look is given directly in the experience of being seen, not confirmed afterward.

forms.stemHtml: Which of the following are among Sartre's three dimensions of the body? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: My body as I live it, passed over in silence
options.text: My body as I live it, passed over in silence
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The first dimension is the body lived, not attended to.

options.html: My body as an object for others
options.text: My body as an object for others
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The second dimension is the body as others perceive it, as an object.

options.html: My body as I exist it as known by others
options.text: My body as I exist it as known by others
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The third dimension is my body lived through the other's look, alienated.

options.html: My body as a situation charged with social meanings
options.text: My body as a situation charged with social meanings
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That's Beauvoir's account of the body as situation, not one of Sartre's three dimensions.

options.html: My body as extended substance, separate from mind
options.text: My body as extended substance, separate from mind
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That's a Cartesian view, which Sartre rejects. It isn't one of his three dimensions.

forms.stemHtml: What is Beauvoir's term for the whole context in which a free existence finds itself and acts: body, history, economic conditions, and social meanings, all as lived? Enter one word.

options.feedbackHtml: Correct! For Beauvoir, the body is not a thing but a situation.

forms.defaultFeedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Beauvoir's term is "situation."

forms.stemHtml: Which statement best captures a key difference between Sartre and Beauvoir on freedom?

options.html: Sartre denies freedom, while Beauvoir affirms it
options.text: Sartre denies freedom, while Beauvoir affirms it
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Both affirm freedom. The difference is whether situations can restrict freedom itself.

options.html: Beauvoir holds that freedom exists only for women
options.text: Beauvoir holds that freedom exists only for women
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Beauvoir holds that freedom is situated, and that situations such as oppression can restrict it.

options.html: Beauvoir holds that situations can restrict freedom
options.text: Beauvoir holds that situations can restrict freedom
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! For Sartre, freedom always transcends the situation. For Beauvoir, situations such as oppression can restrict freedom itself.

options.html: Sartre ties freedom to one's social position
options.text: Sartre ties freedom to one's social position
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. It's Beauvoir who ties freedom to situation. Sartre treats freedom as absolute.

title: Sartre and Beauvoir on the Body
